title: Pan pipes
summary: Andean pan pipes assembled from published rules, not from a measured instrument: the note set of a zampona (G major), the tube bore scaling of measured panpipes and the lip-jet controls of a player (Fletcher 2005, with the blowing pressure and jet length at each pitch from the flute-player relations of Fletcher 1975), with each tube's length computed from its note and blown one tube at a time as a stopped pipe filled with the gas Coltman measured in a played flute's bore. Speaks; not graded on the site. Screened siku recordings now exist (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0, 26 pitches), but the grader has no library for them yet, so the notes are listened to; G4 and B4 were measured against them with the grader's own functions only (see what is missing). No published table of measured siku or zampona tube lengths could be reached, and nothing here claims to match a real instrument.
physics_present: fs-couple flue_loop: a lip jet acting on a stopped cylindrical tube, with its blowing pressure and jet length at each tube's equal-tempered pitch from Fletcher 1975's measured flute-player relations (p [mbar] = 0.008 nu, l [mm] = 1.8 + 100 nu^(-1/2); 117.5 Pa and 10.05 mm at D3 to 395.1 Pa and 6.30 mm at B4) and its lip height from the published range ends, 1 mm to 0.5 mm, paired linearly in log2 f
the stopped-pipe resonator: closed at the far end, open at the blown top, with the published bore scaling and the open-end correction
the published stopped-pipe jet offset: the closed end blocks the steady flow so the jet passes outside the lip by half a jet half-width, applied as the labium offset
fractional-delay propagation and gas-derived viscothermal loss along the tube
radiation observed at a physical receiver from the open top

the tubes' gas: the gas Coltman measured in a played flute's bore (Physics Today 21(11), 1968, p. 27; ledger coltman-1968-flute-bore-gas), as the three flute cards carry it: the explicit mixture at 26.15 C (299.30 K), 101325 Pa, saturated, 2.5 percent dry CO2 and 18.5 percent dry O2, with the observer and radiation exterior kept as dry air at 20 C. It is a measurement of a flute bore applied to stopped pipes by analogy, not of a played pan pipe, and a stopped tube may exchange far less breath, so the real fill may lie closer to room air: the bracket runs from dry 20 C air to this state (unknowns u-bore-gas). Measured with the card controls of u-player-controls, on one binary, it raises every tube by 16.6 to 16.7 cents over dry 20 C air and by 5.4 to 5.5 cents over the shared woodwind pack the cards carried before (27 C, 4.5 percent dry CO2); the level and the grader's envelope, harmonic and combined spectral distances to a recording move by no more than 0.1 dB, and the render's HNR stays at the solver's numerical floor (79 dB) because it has no noise

the player's jet controls are a law measured on flute players, applied to a stopped pipe by analogy, as Fletcher 2005 does for the jet speed: neither paper measures a pan-pipe player, D3 lies below every pitch the source reports and G3 is the alto flute's lowest note, covered by an unplotted sentence. Against the previous controls (the range ends paired linearly in log2 f) the pressure is 0.40 to 0.49 of theirs and the jet length 1 to 26 percent longer; every note still speaks its first register under the card's jet, 13 to 18 cents flatter and 7 to 10 dB quieter. Against the sikus (G4 and B4) the grader's combined spectral distance falls by 0.5 to 2.2 dB and the centroid ratio by about a quarter, and the render is still 2.3 to 5.2 times too bright. Under the forced Bickley jet (an opt-in row on no card) these controls and the previous ones both sound the third register, and the seventh at B4, so the controls do not decide the register there (unknowns u-player-controls)
a self-sustained oscillation: each tube settles to a steady tone and re-rendering with another jet seed gives the same pitch and level
physics_missing: a graded comparison: screened siku recordings exist (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0, 26 pitches, 44 valid clips), but the grader's library is built from UIowa-named files and holds none of them, so no pair is graded and the site shows these notes as listening only. Measured directly with the grader's own functions (instrgrade-4, no real-vs-real ruler), G4 against three sikus and B4 against one, the renders sit far from the recordings: spectral centroid 2.3 to 5.2 times too high, upper-harmonic share 9 to 21 dB too high, and an HNR of 79 dB against the recordings' 9 to 22 dB, because the render has no breath noise. No claim of resemblance is made

measured tube lengths and bores of a real siku or zampona: the lengths are computed from the notes and the bore from a regression on European panpipes. Andean tubes are much less regular, so this is a design from published rules, not a model of an instrument

the even harmonics the published offset should produce: the renders sound odd harmonics only, with a bright, nearly flat run of upper harmonics where a pan pipe has a dominant fundamental. The island's jet is driven hard into saturation by its authored displacement gain and the offset is small beside the swing, so it has no effect; the same limitation as on the flute

pitch: with the flute's bore gas in the tubes and the flute-player controls the notes land 17.5 to 23.5 cents flat of the tempered design (D3 -17.5, G3 -18.5, D4 -18.5, G4 -18.9, B4 -23.5; with the shared woodwind pack -22.9 to -29.0 and with dry air -34.1 to -40.2; with the previous controls -8.6 to -11.3 with the pack and -19.6 to -22.3 with dry air, the jet pulling the pitch further flat at the lower pressure). The tube lengths were cut for the speed of sound in dry 20 C air (unknowns u-tube-lengths), and the mouth end correction of the jet and the lip is not the thin-wall value used to cut them. Real sikus are not tuned to equal temperament either: the three G4 recordings measure -12.2, -29.1 and -28.4 cents and the one B4 recording +36.7 cents of the tempered note, so the mean distance of the G4 render from them is 8.8 cents (7.0 with the shared pack, 8.1 with dry air and the previous controls, 13.2 with the pack and the previous controls) and of the B4 render 60.2 cents (65.7 with the shared pack, 59.0 and 48.0 with the previous controls)

the jet: the card is an estimate for a lip jet, not a measured jet card, and the jet is only 5.0 to 6.3 times its height (5.03 at D3, 5.08 G3, 5.34 D4, 5.76 G4, 6.30 B4), under the 5.6 where the island's phase correction is exact for D3, G3 and D4 and over it for G4 and B4; the displacement gain is the demonstrator value, the lip aperture width is taken as the tube width, and the jet spreading across the top of the tube is not modelled
the percussive Andean playing style with a turbulent jet; only the normal laminar style is rendered
neighbouring tubes: they are not coupled, nor is the array radiation or the player's lips and face
onset ramp, mouth loss and breath noise: authored, neutral or absent (the bore's gas is Coltman 1968's played-flute state, unknowns u-bore-gas)
a radiating outlet at the closed end: the generic input needs one radiating outlet, so a tiny vent of a vanishing fraction of the bore area stands in for it
native verification beyond a single clock and two jet seeds on two notes
